INT. LEARNING    REFLECTIONS    RESUME   


I’ve always been a big fan of personal projects. Some of my most most valuable skills I’ve learned have been through hard-won battles with finicky electronics or curiosity-driven deep dives, all on my own time and dollar.

But the best engineers I know, blend theory and application, built on top of a strong foundation of curiosity. In other words, being I able say “I wonder what happens if…” while also being able to analyze and explain any (potentially disastrous) consequences

I’ve had my fair share of failures and successes when it comes to my own personal projects. Here are some of my more notable entires.

Crystal FPGA Board

I've been involved with the EE478 Digital Design course at SUNY University at Buffalo for a number of years now. In 2025, I even had the pleasure of being a temporary adjunct professor and teaching the class for part of the year. This course deals primarily focuses on FPGAs, with students renting a Xilinx Zybo board from the department. Every year, there are always a handful of promising students who want to keep experimenting with their FPGAs. These boards are expensive, so the department must inevitably yank them away.

This is not a unique problem to UB. There are essentially zero obtainable alternatives for the average college student. With that in mind, I been developing the Crystal FPGA Board. The board is based on a Lattice CrossLink-NX and is compatible with the Adafruit Feather ecosystem and comes in at a $50 price point - about half the cost of the norm. If you'd like to learn more I have project logs on my project page

I'm also very proud to say that the project was covered by Hackster.io!

Cyborg-Eyeball Project

This is one of those "I wonder if I could..." projects that ultimately didn't lead anywhere but made some for great pictures and received a decent amount of attention. I've always had an interest in all things cyberpunk and bio-hacking. When it comes to the cyberpunk aesthetic, nothing can beat a pair of glowing, digital eyes. I knew it was a silly, somewhat dangerous idea. To all the concerned citizens of the internet that commented on the well being of my eyeballs my response with steadfast: "I'm risking my eyeballs so you don't have to!"

Evidently this project was flashy enough to attact the attention of PC Gamer magazine with the headline of:

This real life Cyberpunk 2077 eye mod makes my skin crawl


Fair enough.

Computationally Assessing Diamond as an Ultrafast Pulse Shaper

During my undergraduate degree, I had the privilege of conducting research on behalf of Michigan State University. My work involved performing TCAD simulations of diamond-based diodes under Sergey Baryshev. These devices could be used to create ultra-fast (10s of picoseconds), very high power pulses of electrical energy, which is extremely useful in the field of power electronics and radar.

Diamond is considered to be a wide-bandgap semiconductor (the widest, actually) and is theoretically the most thermal conductivity material possible. Combine this with a very high electron-mobility and extreme tolerance to high-voltage breakdown, it’s a prime candidate for future high power semiconductor devices.

While not exactly a personal project, this effort is one of those unique experiences that not only helped me learn some deeply interesting physics, but also gave me a unique edge in my professional life.

We even managed to get a paper published on the topic. Not bad for an undergrad!
